23 An electromagnetic wave has a wavelength of 2.1 cm in a vacuum.
Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum contains this wave?
A
infrared
B
microwave
C
radio wave
D
visible light

hints: Convert the given $2.1 \text{ cm}$ into metres to compare with standard spectrum values: $2.1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.
Recall the order of increasing wavelength around this size: infrared below about $1 \text{ mm}$, then microwaves from about $1 \text{ mm}$ to $10 \text{ cm}$, then radio waves above that.
Check whether $2.1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ fits below $1 \text{ mm}$, between $1 \text{ mm}$ and $10 \text{ cm}$, or above $10 \text{ cm}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given quantity: wavelength $\lambda = 2.1 \text{ cm}$ in vacuum.
Convert to SI units: $\lambda = 2.1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 21 \text{ mm}$.

Recall approximate boundaries: infrared is roughly $10^{-6} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-3} \text{ m}$, microwaves roughly $10^{-3} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-1} \text{ m}$, radio waves greater than $10^{-1} \text{ m}$, and visible light about $10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
Compare $2.1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ with these ranges: it is larger than $10^{-3} \text{ m}$ but smaller than $10^{-1} \text{ m}$.
Therefore it falls in the microwave region. This is option B.

A.explanation: Infrared wavelengths are much shorter, typically about $10^{-6} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-3} \text{ m}$, so $2.1 \text{ cm}$ is too long.

B.explanation: A wavelength of $2.1 \text{ cm}$ equals $2.1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, which lies in the microwave range of about $10^{-3} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-1} \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: Radio waves have longer wavelengths, typically greater than about $10^{-1} \text{ m}$, so $2.1 \text{ cm}$ is too short.

D.explanation: Visible light has wavelengths around $4 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, far shorter than $2.1 \text{ cm}$.
